title: Data Residency & Cross-Region Cost
summary: Locality law and cross-region egress cost are first-class design inputs, not afterthoughts bolted on after legal or finance objects to the ideal topology.

slides.markdown:
Two forces routinely get discovered *after* a multi-region design is already drawn: **data residency** (law dictating where data may physically live) and **cross-region cost** (what replicating and moving data between regions actually costs on the bill).

Both are design inputs, not footnotes — a topology that ignores residency law can be flatly illegal, and one that ignores egress cost can be technically correct but financially unworkable. This topic treats both as first-class constraints from the start.

slides.sectionTitle: Data residency: why some data legally cannot leave a region
slides.markdown:
**Data residency** is a legal or regulatory requirement that certain data physically stay within a specific country or bloc's borders — not encrypted-in-transit-through, not backed-up-elsewhere, but stored and processed within that boundary. It typically applies to categories like personal data, health records, or financial records, and the rules come from national or regional law, not from the cloud provider.

This is fundamentally different from every other force covered in this group: latency and availability are engineering trade-offs you can choose to accept, but residency is a hard constraint — violating it isn't a performance regression, it's a legal and compliance failure with real penalties.

The practical consequence: residency has to be checked before a topology is chosen, not layered on afterward — a design built around free replication everywhere may need to be partially undone.

slides.sectionTitle: GDPR-style locality constraints as a system design input
slides.markdown:
GDPR-style regulation is the canonical example: EU personal data has restrictions on transfer outside the EU, and similar country-specific rules exist elsewhere — data-localization laws in several countries require certain categories of data to stay within national borders entirely.

As a design input, this means a system serving EU users needs an EU region that actually stores EU personal data at rest, and any cross-region replication of that data has to either stop at the EU boundary or go through an approved legal mechanism — it isn't solved by choosing a nearby-but-non-EU region for latency reasons alone.

The interview-relevant move is to treat this as a partitioning question early: which categories of data are residency-constrained, and which regions can legally hold each category — before deciding topology or replication strategy for anything else.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a design partitioned by residency boundary
slides.markdown:
![EU and US regions each wall off their own user data behind a residency boundary, bridged by a shared non-personal metadata and analytics store](assets/residency-boundary.svg)

The partition here isn't drawn by load or latency — it's drawn by legal category. EU personal data stays inside the EU box; non-personal or aggregated data can cross freely, since residency law targets specific data categories, not the whole system.

This is why residency-aware designs often look like several independent regional systems for the constrained data, bridged by a shared layer for everything that isn't.

slides.sectionTitle: Cross-region replication traffic and egress cost: the real bill
slides.markdown:
Every byte replicated from one region to another typically incurs **egress cost** — cloud providers charge for data leaving a region, often while charging little or nothing for data arriving. A system replicating a high-write-volume database continuously across three regions can rack up a meaningfully sized monthly bill purely from that replication traffic, separate from any compute or storage cost.

This scales with write volume and replica count, not with read traffic — a system with heavy writes and many regions pays proportionally more, which is exactly why active-active topologies (every region writing, replicating to every other region) tend to cost more in egress than a single-writer topology replicating one direction.

The practical habit: when estimating multi-region cost, egress needs its own line item next to compute and storage, not an assumption that it's negligible.

| | Replicate everything | Replicate only what residency allows |
|---|---|---|
| Legal risk | High if any residency-constrained data crosses a boundary | Low — constrained data never leaves its legal boundary |
| Egress cost | Highest — full dataset replicated to every region | Lower — only non-constrained data crosses regions |
| Read latency for constrained data elsewhere | Fast everywhere, since it's fully replicated | Slower or unavailable outside the home region, by design |
| Engineering complexity | Simpler — one replication policy for all data | Higher — data has to be classified and routed by category |

**How to decide:** classify data by residency category before deciding replication policy; only data cleared to cross a boundary should be replicated broadly, and accept the added classification complexity as the cost of staying both legal and reasonably cheap to run.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: designing the ideal active-active topology, then discovering residency forbids it
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Let's design the best-performing active-active topology first, then handle compliance requirements afterward."

**Why it's wrong:** active-active by definition replicates writes bidirectionally between every participating region — if any of that data is residency-constrained, the topology itself may be illegal the moment it's built, and "add compliance later" often means partially undoing the replication design rather than adjusting a config flag. Unlike latency or cost, residency isn't a spectrum you can tune after the fact; a violation already happened the moment constrained data crossed the boundary.

**Correct model:** classify data by residency requirement before choosing a topology, not after. Design the constrained data's placement first, then layer performance-oriented topology decisions like active-active on top of whatever data is actually free to move.
